# Test Lab: A Stateless Data-Prep Toolbox

## 🧰 The Analogy: A Workbench, Not a Sandbox

The **Test Lab** is a workbench of independent tools, not an interactive wrangling sandbox. There is no
action-picker UI, no stacked pipeline you build node by node, and no persistent working state between
tools (`.claude/rules/rules_test_lab.md §1`, ADR-084). Each tool runs to completion and hands you back a
downloadable file. Close the panel and the tool resets to empty — nothing is remembered except the named
files you explicitly save.

This is a deliberate contrast with **Blueprint Architect** (nicknamed "Wrangle Studio" elsewhere in this
book — see `Terminology.qmd`), which *is* the space where wrangling, joins, and plot authoring happen as a
persistent, saved recipe. Test Lab never authors `tier1`/`tier2` wrangling logic or plot specs; it only
prepares the raw files a scientist hands to that pipeline. The "Audit Stack" (the T3 right-sidebar panel
in HOME that records row filters, exclusions, and column drops with a mandatory reason) is a real feature
of a different space entirely — it has no connection to Test Lab.

## 🛠️ Purpose: Removing Data-Prep Friction Before the Pipeline Runs

Scientists routinely hit a handful of unglamorous blockers before their data analysis recipe can even be
written: files arrive as multi-sheet Excel workbooks, two collaborators' files disagree on sample ID
formatting, a pipeline needs a shareable dataset that doesn't expose real identities, and a new data
source needs a first-pass schema sketch before anyone touches BLUEPRINT. Test Lab exists to clear these
blockers, each with its own tool, each independent of the others:

1. **AquaSynthesizer** — reads a real TSV and emits a structurally identical *synthetic* TSV: same column
   names, same value distributions and levels, different values. Safe to share, and also used to generate
   controlled-error datasets for exercising pipeline edge cases without ever touching real data.
2. **Data Analysis Recipe Bootstrapper/Scaffolder** — infers column types and cardinalities from a TSV and
   writes a boilerplate `input_fields` YAML fragment (Bootstrapper), or turns a batch of prepared TSVs
   into a boilerplate data analysis recipe ZIP with structure, inferred types, and PK hints
   (Scaffolder) — eliminating manual schema typing when onboarding a new data source. Neither one writes
   `analysis_groups`, plots, or join strategy; that remains BLUEPRINT's job
   (`.claude/rules/rules_test_lab.md §4`).
3. **ID Reconciliation** (`libs/id_reconciliation/`) — matches a single primary-key column between two
   files (exact, pattern-based, then fuzzy matching) when two collaborators' sample IDs don't line up, and
   produces a reusable id-transformation YAML. Scoped to one key column per pairwise run; composite or
   n-way key matching belongs in BLUEPRINT's Join Designer (`rules_test_lab.md §5`).
4. **Anonymiser** — strips identifying columns and replaces an ID column with a sequential, hash-based, or
   custom-prefix anonymous id, writing an original-id-to-anon-id mapping alongside so the substitution can
   be traced (but not reversed by a reader who only has the anonymised file).
5. **Reformatter / Extractor** — converts XLSX/CSV files to TSV, including multi-sheet Excel workbooks
   split one sheet per output TSV — the practical first step for data that arrives in spreadsheet form.

Each tool is reached independently from the Test Lab panel (gated by `test_lab_enabled`, developer/qa
app features only) and leaves no trace once you move on — only a file you chose to download or a named
scenario you chose to save persists. There is no "ghost-loading" of Gallery examples into Test Lab:
Gallery has no interactive handoff into any other space, Test Lab included (ADR-093).

Test Lab is the bridge between raw, messy files and a data source BLUEPRINT can actually build a recipe
from — not a place to explore or iterate on the analysis itself.
